snippet.title: How Rockefeller BURIED His Competition | The Secret Railroad Deal
snippet.description:
In January 1872, John D. Rockefeller absorbed 22 of Cleveland's 26 oil refineries in 90 days. He didn't outcompete them. He had secretly arranged for the railroads to charge his competitors more than twice what they charged him — and to pay him a cut of what his competitors spent on shipping. The paper trail exists. Most people never followed it.

In this video, we follow the documented story of Standard Oil — from the secret South Improvement Company scheme that launched Rockefeller's monopoly, to the 1911 Supreme Court breakup that made him even richer, and the corporate tactics that trace directly to his playbook today.

SOURCES & FURTHER READING:
1. Ida Tarbell — 'The History of the Standard Oil Company' (1904, McClure's Magazine)
2. Ron Chernow — 'Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller, Sr.' (1998, Random House)
3. US Supreme Court — Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, 221 U.S. 1 (1911)
4. Congressional Record — South Improvement Company Hearings, US House of Representatives (1872)
5. US House Judiciary Committee — 'Investigation of Competition in Digital Markets' (2020)

Wall Street loved it. Business magazines praised his vision. But today, Zulily is dead, QVC is drowning in $6.6 billion of debt, and the $14 billion shopping empire is facing bankruptcy.

This is the story of one of retail's most catastrophic acquisitions—a tale of mismatched business models, clashing corporate cultures, and a CEO who escaped just before everything collapsed. Did Mike George's Zulily purchase destroy QVC? Or was this retail giant already doomed by cord-cutting and Amazon's dominance?

• Mike George acquired Zulily for $2.4 billion in 2015—QVC sold it for essentially nothing in 2023

• George retired in October 2021, just before the collapse accelerated
